sections.section_title: The Journey and the Test Case
sections.summary: Paul narrates going up to Jerusalem after fourteen years with Barnabas and the uncircumcised Greek Titus, who was not compelled to be circumcised, and reports that he gave no ground to infiltrators who came to spy out the freedom believers have in Christ Jesus and to enslave them.

The reputed leaders added no requirement to Paul's message, recognized that the same God was at work in his mission to the uncircumcised as in Peter's to the circumcised, sealed a division of mission fields with the right hand of fellowship, and asked only that the Gentile mission remember the poor.

Paul publicly opposed Cephas at Antioch because Cephas, whose settled practice had been to eat with Gentile believers, drew back and separated himself out of fear when men came from James, and Paul charged that this withdrawal — though it commanded nothing — functioned as compulsion on Gentiles to Judaize, since it left conversion as the only route back to full fellowship.

The letter's hinge states, as something already held in common between Paul and Peter, that a person is not reckoned in the right by works of law but through the faith(fulness) of Jesus Christ, closing with an adapted citation of Psalm 143:2 that no flesh will be justified by works of law.
sections.relevance: The verse locates the basis of a favourable verdict outside anything the person performs — three times over — which is the standard ground for arguing that standing so established cannot be forfeited by subsequent performance; the sustained emphatic "we" makes the claim about Jews, not only about Gentile admission, so it cannot be confined to entry terms. Two things in the neutral reading blunt that use, however: dikaioo is a courtroom word whose timing the verse does not specify — Paul uses it both as accomplished and as awaited ("we await the hope of righteousness," 5:5) — and if pistis Iesou Christou is Christ's own faithfulness rather than the believer's trust, the permanence implication strengthens, while on the objective reading the securing element is a human act. The verse is a claim about the basis of the verdict, not about its retention, and it does not adjudicate its own contested terms.
key_phrases: a person is not justified by works of law
even we believed in Christ Jesus
by works of law no flesh will be justified

sections.section_title: Died to Law, Alive to God
sections.summary: Paul rejects the inference that Christ serves sin if Jews seeking justification in Christ are found in the sinners' category, says that rebuilding what he tore down would make him the transgressor, describes a participatory death to law that leaves Christ living in him, and closes with a reductio: if righteousness comes through law, Christ died for nothing.
sections.relevance: The load-bearing statements of Paul's own argument point toward permanence: the crucifixion with Christ is a compound verb in the perfect tense — a completed event whose effect is his present condition — the living agent is now Christ rather than Paul, and the ground named is one who "loved me and gave himself for me," a finished act. Cutting the other way, the life is still lived "by faith of the Son of God" in ongoing present tense, and v. 21's atheteo ("render void, annul") together with v. 18's rebuilding logic supplies the framework the letter later turns into the explicit warning of 5:4. But the neutral reading is specific that the transgression in v. 18 is the reimposition of the Jew-Gentile separation, not apostasy, and that v. 21 is Paul returning an accusation rather than warning that grace can be lost — so the conditional side of the passage is inference from its terms rather than its stated argument.
key_phrases: if I rebuild what I tore down, I prove myself a transgressor
through law I died to law, so that I might live to God
I have been crucified with Christ
it is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me
I live by faith of the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me
I do not nullify the grace of God
if righteousness comes through law, then Christ died for nothing
